newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss minister defies quit call for offending Jews.
newsitem.headline: Swiss minister defies quit call for offending Jews.

text.p: Switzerland's economics minister defied a demand by the country's biggest coalition party on Saturday that he quit for describing as "blackmail" Jewish calls for Swiss restitution to Holocaust victims.

The executive board of the Social Democrats (SP), one of four parties in the centre-left coalition that has ruled since 1959, adopted a resolution accusing Jean-Pascal Delamuraz of unleashing a wave of anti-Semitism and urging him to step down.
Delamuraz, a Radical Democrat (FDP), said in a statement the demand was "unacceptable" and accused the SP of exploiting the crisis to reap political gain.

Delamuraz has since apologised for the remarks he made in a newspaper interview last month as he finished a one-year term in the rotating Swiss presidency. He said he based his comment on inaccurate information.

SP parliamentary deputies Jean-Nils de Dardel and Paul Rechsteiner said in their motion in Berne that Delamuraz's comments used "the worst anti-Semitic stereotype" and made expressing anti-Jewish sentiment nearly respectable.
FDP party president Franz Steinegger described the resignation call to Swiss radio as a "dumb move that damages Switzerland".

"This attempt to turn Delamuraz into a Nazi will fail miserably," he told Swiss television, adding that the motion only aggravated Swiss ties to Jewish groups that are slowly improving after worsening badly because of the incident.
The SP motion urged the cabinet to distance itself from Delamuraz's remarks, something it has refused so far to do.

Delamuraz's comments outraged Israeli politicians and world Jewish groups, prompting them to renew threats of a boycott against Swiss banks. They dropped the threats after Delamuraz said he was very sorry for his remarks.

His apology was much more clear-cut in the English-language version of a letter he wrote the head of the World Jewish Congress (WJC) than in the German and French translations, but Jewish groups were satisfied and have resumed talks.

Berne politicians say it would be extremely unusual for the cabinet to chastise Delamuraz considering Switzerland's political culture, which emphasises consensus over confrontation as a way of holding the multi-ethnic country together.

It was also unlikely because of a perception in Berne that Delamuraz's views were shared by a lot of ordinary Swiss, many of whose letters to newspapers have scorned Jewish restitution efforts as a way of extorting money from wealthy Switzerland.
Groups led by the WJC say the Swiss profited cynically from World War Two by sitting on accounts left ownerless by Jewish victims and by buying looted gold from Nazi Germany.
The government and leading businesses have agreed in principle to create a holocaust memorial fund, but details have yet to be worked out.
The Social Democrats have two of the seven cabinet seats. The rest are held by three conservative parties. Cabinet members are basically autonomous and do not have to follow party appeals.
